hints: Match each reagent to the functional group it tests for, Z contains an alkene and carboxyl groups, so think about what type of reaction each reagent gives.
Recall the starting colour of aqueous bromine and what visible change shows a gas is evolved from a solid carbonate.
walkthrough:
Link bromine water to the C=C bond**
Think about what bromine water does. It is orange in colour. When it meets a C=C double bond it adds across the bond in an electrophilic addition reaction. The $\text{Br}_2$ is used up, so its orange colour disappears and the solution becomes colourless. Since Z contains an alkene group, you see orange to colourless.

Link carbonate solid to the COOH group**
Think about what a carboxylic acid does to a carbonate. Acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide gas: $2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The visible sign is fizzing or bubbles or effervescence as $\text{CO}_2$ escapes. Since Z contains carboxyl groups, solid $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ fizzes.

Final answer: $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$: orange to colourless (orange disappears).
$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(s)}$: fizzing / bubbles / effervescence.

hints: Convert each percentage by mass into moles by dividing by the relative atomic mass ($\text{C}=12$, $\text{H}=1$, $\text{O}=16$) and then compare the simplest ratio.
walkthrough:
Divide by $A_r$ to get moles**
Imagine 100 g of Z, so the percentages become masses in grams. Moles = mass / $A_r$:
$$n(\text{C}) = 41.38/12 = 3.448$$
$$n(\text{H}) = 3.45/1 = 3.45$$
$$n(\text{O}) = 55.17/16 = 3.448$$
All three values are essentially 3.45, so divide each by the smallest (3.45) to give $1:1:1$. That proves the empirical formula is $\text{CHO}$.
Final answer: $\text{C} : \text{H} : \text{O} = 41.38/12 : 3.45/1 : 55.17/16 = 3.45 : 3.45 : 3.45 = 1:1:1$, so empirical formula is $\text{CHO}$.

hints: Identify the molecular ion peak ($M^+$) at the highest $m/e$ with significant abundance in Fig. 6.1 and calculate the mass of one CHO unit to compare.
walkthrough:
Read $M_r$ then scale up the empirical formula**
In a mass spectrum the peak at the largest $m/e$ (ignoring the tiny $M+1$ isotope peak at 117) is the molecular ion, $\text{M}^+$. Here that is $m/e = 116$, so $M_r(\text{Z}) = 116$. One $\text{CHO}$ unit has mass $12 + 1 + 16 = 29$. Calculate:
$$116/29 = 4$$
So the molecule contains 4 empirical units: $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$.
Final answer: Molecular ion peak at $m/e = 116$, so $M_r = 116$. Mass of $\text{CHO} = 12+1+16 = 29$. $116/29 = 4$, so molecular formula $= \text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$.

hints: For each $m/e$ value, try combinations of C, H and O that add to that mass, remembering Z contains only $\text{C}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{O}$ and has carboxyl groups.
Check that mass 45 fits a common oxygen rich acid fragment, and mass 71 fits what remains after losing 45 from the molecular mass of 116.
walkthrough:
Assign $m/e$ 45**
Add up atoms to make 45. With C, H and O only, $12 + 1 + 16 \times 2 = 45$. That is exactly the carboxyl cation:
$$[\text{COOH}]^+$$
This is a very common fragment for carboxylic acids and fits with Z containing COOH groups. It is the base peak (tallest), showing it is a stable fragment.

Assign $m/e$ 71**
Do the same for 71. Try $\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{O}_2$: $(3 \times 12) + (3 \times 1) + (2 \times 16) = 36 + 3 + 32 = 71$. So the ion is:
$$[\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{O}_2]^+$$
Notice $116 - 45 = 71$, so this fragment corresponds to loss of one $\text{COOH}$ group from the molecular ion, which supports a dicarboxylic acid structure.

hints: Combine the molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$ with the need for one C=C bond and two COOH groups, then arrange the four carbons in a chain that satisfies both.
walkthrough:
Build the only structure that fits all the evidence**
Pull the clues together. Formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$ with only alkene and carboxyl groups means you need two $\text{COOH}$ groups (that uses $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$) plus a $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$ alkene unit left over. Join them as:
$$\text{HOOCCH=CHCOOH}$$
This is butenedioic acid. It contains one C=C (explains bromine water decolourisation) and two COOH groups (explains fizzing with carbonate and the $m/e$ 45 fragment). Either the cis/Z or trans/E form is accepted.
Final answer: $\text{HOOCCH=CHCOOH}$ (trans / E-butenedioic acid or cis / Z-butenedioic acid).
